items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “how far a source or claim can be believed, judged by criteria such as expertise, reputation and vested interest”?
items.answer: Credibility
items.markingKey: Credibility: how far a source or claim can be believed, judged by criteria such as expertise, reputation and vested interest. [1]

items.stem: Assess the credibility of a campaign report produced by an NGO as a source of information on lowering the voting age to 16.
items.answer: Strength: the NGO has field experience of the issue. Weakness: its purpose is partly to persuade and raise funds, so it may select evidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark strength, 1 mark explained using a credibility criterion; 1 mark weakness, 1 mark explained [4]

items.stem: A student finds a study by a university research centre with no funding from interested parties about state use of facial recognition surveillance. Explain one strength and one weakness of this source’s credibility.
items.answer: Strength: its authors have expertise and no obvious vested interest. Weakness: it may use a small or local sample.
items.markingKey: 1 mark strength, 1 mark explained using a credibility criterion; 1 mark weakness, 1 mark explained [4]

items.stem: A student researching disputes over shared rivers finds a press release from a company that would profit from the policy, published in 2019. It states: “Reduced water for irrigation downstream.” Make a judgement about how far the claim can be trusted.
items.answer: Judgement weighing the strength and weakness above and the need for corroboration.
items.markingKey: 1 mark judgement; 1 mark supported by two criteria [2]

items.stem: A student researching the under-representation of women in parliaments finds an article in an established international newspaper, published in 2025. It states: “A country scores poorly in international gender equality rankings.” (a) Suggest how the student could check the claim. (b) Make a judgement about how far the claim can be trusted.
items.answer: (a) Look for corroboration in an independent source, e.g. official statistics or a peer-reviewed study, and check the date and original data. (b) Judgement weighing the strength and weakness above and the need for corroboration.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark corroboration; 1 mark specific type of source [2] (b) 1 mark judgement; 1 mark supported by two criteria [2]

items.stem: A student researching corruption in public procurement finds a personal blog by a student with no stated sources, published in 2019. It states: “Foreign investors avoid countries seen as corrupt.” (a) Identify one feature of the source that increases its credibility. (b) Identify one feature of the source that reduces its credibility.
items.answer: (a) It may reflect a genuine personal experience. (b) It has no expertise or sources to check.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark feature; 1 mark linked to criterion [2] (b) 1 mark feature; 1 mark linked to criterion [2]

items.stem: On threats to press freedom, Source A is a report by an intergovernmental organisation such as the UN Development Programme; Source B is a personal blog by a student with no stated sources. The two sources reach different conclusions. (a) Explain one weakness of Source B’s credibility. (b) Explain one limitation of Source A.
items.answer: (a) It has no expertise or sources to check. (b) It may avoid openly criticising member governments.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark weakness; 1 mark criterion [2] (b) 1 mark limitation; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: On threats to press freedom, Source A is a study by a university research centre with no funding from interested parties; Source B is a press release from a company that would profit from the policy. The two sources reach different conclusions. (a) Explain one strength of Source A’s credibility. (b) Explain one weakness of Source B’s credibility. (c) Explain one limitation of Source A.
items.answer: (a) Its authors have expertise and no obvious vested interest. (b) It has a clear vested interest. (c) It may use a small or local sample.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark strength; 1 mark criterion [2] (b) 1 mark weakness; 1 mark criterion [2] (c) 1 mark limitation; 1 mark developed [2]

items.answer: Credibility

items.stem: A student finds a personal blog by a student with no stated sources about disputes over shared rivers. Explain one strength and one weakness of this source’s credibility.
items.answer: Strength: it may reflect a genuine personal experience. Weakness: it has no expertise or sources to check.
items.markingKey: 1 mark strength, 1 mark explained using a credibility criterion; 1 mark weakness, 1 mark explained [4]

items.stem: In a statement published on its website, a waste trading company says it argues the trade supplies raw materials. The statement adds that it earns profits from shipping waste. Explain how a vested interest might affect the credibility of this source.
items.answer: The source argues the trade supplies raw materials; it earns profits from shipping waste, so it may select evidence that supports its position and leave out evidence against it. Its claims need corroboration from a neutral source.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies the interest; 1 mark explains likely effect on claims; 1 mark need for corroboration [3]

items.stem: A student researching threats to press freedom finds a peer-reviewed article in an academic political science journal, published in 2023. It states: “Self-censorship among journalists.” Explain how the date of publication affects the usefulness of the source.
items.answer: Published in 2023: recent enough to be relevant only if the situation has not changed since; the student should check for newer data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark currency; 1 mark applied [2]

items.stem: Explain whether you agree that official government sources are the most credible sources of information about corruption in public procurement. Give one reason for and one reason against.
items.answer: For: Governments collect large-scale data through statistics offices. Ministers have access to official information. Against: Governments have vested interests, e.g. Transparency International campaigns for open contracting and stronger enforcement. Independent academic studies and international bodies may be more neutral. Judgement: Credibility depends on the type of claim and the government’s independence; corroboration across sources is the best test.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (2 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (3–4 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [4]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a personal story or individual experience used as evidence”?
items.answer: Anecdote
items.markingKey: Anecdote: a personal story or individual experience used as evidence. [1]

items.stem: Read this evidence about low voter turnout among young people: “A campaign group in Dubai predicts that, if nothing is done by 2040, this effect will become far more serious: “Elected governments can claim less legitimacy”.” Explain one strength and one weakness of this evidence.
items.answer: Prediction. Strength: it warns about possible future consequences. Weakness: it cannot be verified yet and comes from a campaign group with a purpose.
items.markingKey: 1 mark strength, 1 mark developed; 1 mark weakness, 1 mark developed [4]

items.stem: Read this evidence about reform of the UN Security Council: “A survey of 800 adults in Zentara found that 32% think the UN member states should abolish or restrict the veto for cases of mass atrocities.” Explain one strength and one weakness of this evidence.
items.answer: Statistic. Strength: it is based on a large sample, so it is more representative than one example. Weakness: we do not know how the sample was chosen or how the question was worded.
items.markingKey: 1 mark strength, 1 mark developed; 1 mark weakness, 1 mark developed [4]

items.stem: A campaign group in Esteria claims that “most citizens” support the proposal that the UN member states should abolish or restrict the veto for cases of mass atrocities. Its evidence: 356 of 600 people who took part in a phone-in on a radio show agreed. Esteria has about 30 million adults. Calculate the percentage who agreed and the sample as a percentage of the adult population.
items.markingKey: 1 mark agreement %; 1 mark sample as % of population [2]

items.stem: A campaign group in Merania claims that “most citizens” support the proposal that the United Nations member states should extend refugee protection to people displaced by climate change. Its evidence: 103 of 150 people who took part in a phone-in on a radio show agreed. Merania has about 4 million adults. Calculate the percentage who agreed and the sample as a percentage of the adult population. Evaluate whether the evidence supports the claim.
items.answer: 103/150 × 100 = 68.7%; sample = 150/4 million × 100 = 0.0037% of adults (about 0.0037%). The result shows majority support among respondents, but the sample is tiny and self-selected/unrepresentative (a phone-in on a radio show), so it does not show what “most citizens” think.
items.markingKey: 1 mark agreement %; 1 mark sample as % of population; 1 mark sample not representative (method); 1 mark size/self-selection; 1 mark judgement [5]

items.stem: A campaign group in Istrana claims that “most citizens” support the proposal that the national government should require platforms to label and remove false political content. Its evidence: 214 of 300 people who took part in interviews outside a university in the capital agreed. Istrana has about 12 million adults. Calculate the percentage who agreed and the sample as a percentage of the adult population. Evaluate whether the evidence supports the claim.
items.answer: 214/300 × 100 = 71.3%; sample = 300/12 million × 100 = 0.0025% of adults (about 0.0025%). The result shows majority support among respondents, but the sample is tiny and self-selected/unrepresentative (interviews outside a university in the capital), so it does not show what “most citizens” think.
items.markingKey: 1 mark agreement %; 1 mark sample as % of population; 1 mark sample not representative (method); 1 mark size/self-selection; 1 mark judgement [5]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that statistics are always more reliable than personal testimony as evidence about the spread of online disinformation during elections? Consider different perspectives in your answer.
items.answer: For: Large, representative samples can be generalised. Statistics can be checked and compared over time. Against: Statistics can be biased by sampling, question wording or presentation. Testimony shows experience and causes that numbers miss, e.g. eyewitnesses with ability to see. Judgement: Reliability depends on how the evidence was produced; the strongest case uses statistics and testimony that corroborate each other.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Read this evidence about threats to press freedom: “A survey of 800 adults in Merania found that 75% think the parliament should protect journalists’ sources and repeal broad “false news” laws.” Explain one strength and one weakness of this evidence.
items.answer: Statistic. Strength: it is based on a large sample, so it is more representative than one example. Weakness: we do not know how the sample was chosen or how the question was worded.
items.markingKey: 1 mark strength, 1 mark developed; 1 mark weakness, 1 mark developed [4]

items.stem: Which piece of evidence would give the strongest support to a claim about public opinion on the spread of online disinformation during elections?
options: “I talked to my neighbours about the spread of online disinformation during elections and they all agreed with me, so I am sure everyone feels the same,” said Tomás, who lives in Nairobi.
A campaign group in Seoul predicts that, if nothing is done by 2035, this effect will become far more serious: “Trust in election results and in the media falls”.
Whatever the evidence says, the way the world has handled the spread of online disinformation during elections is simply unjust.
A survey of 2,000 adults in Pelora found that 48% think the national government should require platforms to label and remove false political content.
items.answer: A survey of 2,000 adults in Pelora found that 48% think the national government should require platforms to label and remove false political content.
items.markingKey: A large survey is more representative than an anecdote; a value judgement and a prediction are not evidence of current opinion. [1]

items.stem: A briefing on the use of economic sanctions uses three pieces of evidence. E1: “Whatever the evidence says, the way the world has handled the use of economic sanctions is simply unjust.” E2: “Professor Ana, who has researched the use of economic sanctions for many years, believes that sanctions often strengthen rather than weaken the targeted regime.” E3: “A survey of 2,500 adults in Marvona found that 74% think the UN Security Council or regional bodies should use targeted (“smart”) sanctions on named individuals and firms.” Explain why a value judgement cannot be used on its own to prove a claim.
items.answer: It expresses what someone thinks is right or wrong; it cannot be checked as true or false, so it needs reasons and evidence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark not verifiable; 1 mark needs support [2]

items.stem: A campaign group in Halvoria claims that “most citizens” support the proposal that the riverside governments should negotiate a basin-wide water-sharing treaty. Its evidence: 442 of 600 people who took part in a phone-in on a radio show agreed. Halvoria has about 12 million adults. Calculate the percentage who agreed and the sample as a percentage of the adult population. Evaluate whether the evidence supports the claim.
items.answer: 442/600 × 100 = 73.7%; sample = 600/12 million × 100 = 0.0050% of adults (about 0.005%). The result shows majority support among respondents, but the sample is tiny and self-selected/unrepresentative (a phone-in on a radio show), so it does not show what “most citizens” think.
items.markingKey: 1 mark agreement %; 1 mark sample as % of population; 1 mark sample not representative (method); 1 mark size/self-selection; 1 mark judgement [5]

items.answer: Percentage point
items.markingKey: Percentage point: the simple difference between two percentages, e.g. from 40% to 50% is a rise of 10 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Countries with more internet users tend to have higher election turnout. What can be concluded?
options: There is no relationship between the two
There is a correlation, but internet use may not cause higher turnout
items.answer: There is a correlation, but internet use may not cause higher turnout
items.markingKey: Correlation ≠ causation; e.g. income or education could affect both. [1]

items.stem: A poll of 1,000 people reports 52% support with a margin of error of ±3 percentage points. What does this mean?
options: True support is likely to be between 49% and 55%
Exactly 52% of the population supports the policy
items.answer: True support is likely to be between 49% and 55%
items.markingKey: 52 ± 3 = 49–55%; a majority is not certain. [1]

items.stem: Turnout among 18–24-year-olds in Ostrelia rose from 59% at one election to 71% at the next. A minister says turnout “rose by 12%”. What was the percentage increase in turnout?
items.markingKey: Percentage change = (71 − 59) / 59 × 100 = 20.3%; the rise was 12 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Turnout among 18–24-year-olds in Esteria rose from 60% at one election to 65% at the next. A minister says turnout “rose by 5%”. Calculate the change in percentage points and the percentage increase, and explain whether the minister’s statement is accurate.
items.answer: 5 percentage points; (65 − 60)/60 × 100 = 8.3%. The minister confuses percentage points with per cent: the relative increase was 8.3%.
items.markingKey: 1 mark percentage points; 1 mark percentage change; 1 mark explains the confusion [3]

items.stem: Election data for Kestria: Year | 2010 | 2014 | 2018 | 2022. Overall turnout (%) | 59 | 53 | 55 | 52. Turnout aged 18–24 (%) | 34 | 36 | 40 | 37. The People’s Movement argues: “Young people are becoming more and more disengaged from politics, so voting must be made compulsory.” (a) Calculate the gap between overall and youth turnout in each year. (b) Suggest one further piece of data that would help evaluate the argument.
items.answer: (a) 2010: 25 points, 2014: 17 points, 2018: 15 points, 2022: 15 points. (b) Turnout in comparable countries with compulsory voting, or survey data on why young people do not vote.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark method; 1 mark all correct [2] (b) 1 mark data; 1 mark why useful [2]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the percentage of registered voters who cast a vote in an election”?
items.answer: Turnout
items.markingKey: Turnout: the percentage of registered voters who cast a vote in an election. [1]

items.stem: Why might an average (mean) income figure give a misleading picture of a typical citizen?
options: Averages cannot be calculated for incomes
The mean is always lower than the median
A few very high incomes raise the mean above what most people earn
items.answer: A few very high incomes raise the mean above what most people earn
items.markingKey: Skewed distributions: median more representative. [1]

items.stem: In an election in Merania, turnout was 56%. The Civic Platform won 43% of the votes cast and 58% of the seats. The party leader claims “the people have given us a clear mandate”. Calculate the percentage of the registered electorate that voted for the party and use your answer to evaluate the leader’s claim.
items.answer: 43 × 56/100 = 24.1% of the electorate. The party has a majority of seats (58%) but only 43% of votes and about 24% of all registered voters, so the claim of a “clear mandate” is weak; however, it won more votes than any other party under the rules of the system.
items.markingKey: 1 mark method; 1 mark answer; 1 mark challenges claim using the figure [3]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “specialist knowledge or training relevant to the claim being made”?
items.answer: Expertise
items.markingKey: Expertise: specialist knowledge or training relevant to the claim being made. [1]

items.stem: In a statement published on its website, a party official says it prefers selection “on merit”. The statement adds that he believes quotas restrict local members’ choice. Explain how a vested interest might affect the credibility of this source.
items.answer: The source prefers selection “on merit”; he believes quotas restrict local members’ choice, so it may select evidence that supports its position and leave out evidence against it. Its claims need corroboration from a neutral source.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies the interest; 1 mark explains likely effect on claims; 1 mark need for corroboration [3]

items.stem: Speaking at a conference in Kuala Lumpur on reform of the UN Security Council, a representative of a permanent member said that it defends the veto. Explain how a vested interest might affect the credibility of this source.
items.answer: The source defends the veto; it protects its national interests and allies, so it may select evidence that supports its position and leave out evidence against it. Its claims need corroboration from a neutral source.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies the interest; 1 mark explains likely effect on claims; 1 mark need for corroboration [3]

items.answer: Published in 2019: recent enough to be relevant only if the situation has not changed since; the student should check for newer data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark currency; 1 mark applied [2]

items.stem: A student researching the export of plastic waste to poorer countries finds a study by a university research centre with no funding from interested parties, published in 2024. It states: “Plastic leaking into rivers and oceans.” Identify one feature of the source that increases its credibility.
items.answer: Its authors have expertise and no obvious vested interest.
items.markingKey: 1 mark feature; 1 mark linked to criterion [2]

items.answer: (a) The company knows its own products. (b) Look for corroboration in an independent source, e.g. official statistics or a peer-reviewed study, and check the date and original data.

items.stem: On the export of plastic waste to poorer countries, Source A is a peer-reviewed article in an academic political science journal; Source B is a personal blog by a student with no stated sources. The two sources reach different conclusions. (a) Explain one strength of Source A’s credibility. (b) Which source is more credible? Justify your answer.
items.answer: (a) Other experts checked its methods before publication. (b) Usually Source A, because other experts checked its methods before publication, whereas it has no expertise or sources to check; but A’s limitation (it may be several years old or focus on a narrow case) means its findings should still be corroborated.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark strength; 1 mark criterion [2] (b) 1 mark judgement; 2 marks comparison using criteria; 1 mark acknowledges limitation [4]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “numerical data, often collected from a survey or official records”?
items.answer: Statistic
items.markingKey: Statistic: numerical data, often collected from a survey or official records. [1]

items.stem: Which piece of evidence would give the strongest support to a claim about public opinion on the export of plastic waste to poorer countries?

A survey of 1,500 adults in Istrana found that 71% think the parties to the Basel Convention should tighten international rules on plastic waste trade.

items.stem: A revision blog states: “An expert opinion is a fact.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It is a judgement by someone with relevant knowledge; it may be well informed but can still be wrong or disputed.

options: A graph axis that does not start at zero, which can exaggerate differences.
The simple difference between two percentages, e.g. from 40% to 50% is a rise of 10 percentage points.
Per person, calculated by dividing a total by the population.
A statistical relationship between two variables, which does not prove causation.

items.stem: A government reports that crime fell by 20% after it changed how crimes are recorded. What is the main problem with this claim?
options: The change in recording means the figures before and after are not comparable
A 20% fall is too small to matter
The government did not use a graph
items.answer: The change in recording means the figures before and after are not comparable
items.markingKey: Changes in definitions/measurement break comparability. [1]

items.stem: In an election in Jovania, turnout was 70%. The Liberal Democrats won 43% of the votes cast and 52% of the seats. The party leader claims “the people have given us a clear mandate”. What percentage of the registered electorate voted for the party?
items.markingKey: 43% × 70% = 30.1% of the electorate. [1]

items.stem: “Statistics used in debates about the spread of online disinformation during elections tell us more about the people presenting them than about the issue.” To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: Statistics are selected and presented to support a perspective (e.g. truncated axes, percentages vs percentage points). Vested interests affect which data are collected and published. Against: Well-collected statistics from neutral sources (statistics offices, peer-reviewed studies) are strong evidence. Misuse can be detected by checking method, sample and presentation. Judgement: Statistics can be strong evidence, but only when their source, method and presentation are evaluated.

items.markingKey: Reputation: the standing a source has gained from its past record of accuracy or inaccuracy. [1]

items.stem: Speaking at a conference in Accra on lowering the voting age to 16, a representative of a student union said that it supports voting at 16. Explain how a vested interest might affect the credibility of this source.
items.answer: The source supports voting at 16; its members are directly affected, so it may select evidence that supports its position and leave out evidence against it. Its claims need corroboration from a neutral source.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies the interest; 1 mark explains likely effect on claims; 1 mark need for corroboration [3]

items.stem: In a statement published on its website, a human rights NGO says it calls for veto restraint in cases of mass atrocity. The statement adds that it focuses on protecting civilians. Explain how a vested interest might affect the credibility of this source.
items.answer: The source calls for veto restraint in cases of mass atrocity; it focuses on protecting civilians, so it may select evidence that supports its position and leave out evidence against it. Its claims need corroboration from a neutral source.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies the interest; 1 mark explains likely effect on claims; 1 mark need for corroboration [3]

items.stem: A student researching reform of the UN Security Council finds a report by an independent election-monitoring mission, published in 2022. It states: “Countries in Africa feel under-represented, reducing the UN’s legitimacy.” Make a judgement about how far the claim can be trusted.
items.answer: Judgement weighing the strength and weakness above and the need for corroboration.
items.markingKey: 1 mark judgement; 1 mark supported by two criteria [2]

items.stem: A student researching disputes over shared rivers finds an article in an established international newspaper, published in 2024. It states: “Reduced water for irrigation downstream.” Identify one feature of the source that increases its credibility.
items.answer: It has editorial checks and a reputation for accuracy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark feature; 1 mark linked to criterion [2]

items.stem: A student researching lowering the voting age to 16 finds an anonymous post on a social media platform, published in 2023. It states: “Parties pay more attention to education and climate policy.” (a) Identify one feature of the source that increases its credibility. (b) Identify one feature of the source that reduces its credibility.
items.answer: (a) It may give an immediate eyewitness view. (b) The author cannot be identified, so expertise and reputation cannot be checked.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark feature; 1 mark linked to criterion [2] (b) 1 mark feature; 1 mark linked to criterion [2]

items.stem: On the under-representation of women in parliaments, Source A is a report by an intergovernmental organisation such as the UN Development Programme; Source B is an anonymous post on a social media platform. The two sources reach different conclusions. (a) Explain one strength of Source A’s credibility. (b) Explain one weakness of Source B’s credibility. (c) Explain one limitation of Source A.
items.answer: (a) It draws on data from many countries and has a reputation to protect. (b) The author cannot be identified, so expertise and reputation cannot be checked. (c) It may avoid openly criticising member governments.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark strength; 1 mark criterion [2] (b) 1 mark weakness; 1 mark criterion [2] (c) 1 mark limitation; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: On migration caused by climate change, Source A is a report by an independent election-monitoring mission; Source B is a press release from a company that would profit from the policy. The two sources reach different conclusions. (a) Explain one weakness of Source B’s credibility. (b) Which source is more credible? Justify your answer.
items.answer: (a) It has a clear vested interest. (b) Usually Source A, because its observers were present at polling stations and are trained to assess elections, whereas it has a clear vested interest; but A’s limitation (observers can visit only a sample of polling stations) means its findings should still be corroborated.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark weakness; 1 mark criterion [2] (b) 1 mark judgement; 2 marks comparison using criteria; 1 mark acknowledges limitation [4]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the judgement of a person with specialist knowledge”?
items.answer: Expert opinion
items.markingKey: Expert opinion: the judgement of a person with specialist knowledge. [1]

items.stem: Which piece of evidence would give the strongest support to a claim about public opinion on reform of the UN Security Council?
options: A campaign group in Jakarta predicts that, if nothing is done by 2050, this effect will become far more serious: “Countries in Africa feel under-represented, reducing the UN’s legitimacy”.
“I talked to my neighbours about reform of the UN Security Council and they all agreed with me, so I am sure everyone feels the same,” said Chloe, who lives in Jakarta.
Whatever the evidence says, the way the world has handled reform of the UN Security Council is simply unjust.
A survey of 2,500 adults in Esteria found that 55% think the UN member states should abolish or restrict the veto for cases of mass atrocities.
items.answer: A survey of 2,500 adults in Esteria found that 55% think the UN member states should abolish or restrict the veto for cases of mass atrocities.
items.markingKey: A large survey is more representative than an anecdote; a value judgement and a prediction are not evidence of current opinion. [1]

items.stem: In a seminar, a student says: “An anecdote can illustrate a point but cannot prove a general claim.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. One case may be untypical, so it cannot be generalised to a whole population.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: A campaign group in Gorvania claims that “most citizens” support the proposal that the United Nations member states should extend refugee protection to people displaced by climate change. Its evidence: 175 of 250 people who took part in interviews outside a university in the capital agreed. Gorvania has about 6 million adults. Calculate the percentage who agreed and the sample as a percentage of the adult population.
items.markingKey: 1 mark agreement %; 1 mark sample as % of population [2]

items.stem: A briefing on migration caused by climate change uses three pieces of evidence. E1: “Whatever the evidence says, the way the world has handled migration caused by climate change is simply unjust.” E2: “A campaign group in Kuala Lumpur predicts that, if nothing is done by 2040, this effect will become far more serious: “Loss of culture and identity for communities that must relocate”.” E3: “A survey of 1,200 adults in Merania found that 66% think the United Nations member states should extend refugee protection to people displaced by climate change.” Which piece of evidence is weakest? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Usually the anecdote or value judgement: it is not representative or cannot be verified.
items.markingKey: 1 mark choice; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: A briefing on the spread of online disinformation during elections uses three pieces of evidence. E1: ““I talked to my neighbours about the spread of online disinformation during elections and they all agreed with me, so I am sure everyone feels the same,” said Mohammed, who lives in Istanbul.” E2: “A campaign group in Hanoi predicts that, if nothing is done by 2035, this effect will become far more serious: “Trust in election results and in the media falls”.” E3: “Whatever the evidence says, the way the world has handled the spread of online disinformation during elections is simply unjust.” (a) Explain why a value judgement cannot be used on its own to prove a claim. (b) Suggest one further piece of evidence that would strengthen the briefing.
items.answer: (a) It expresses what someone thinks is right or wrong; it cannot be checked as true or false, so it needs reasons and evidence. (b) A large representative survey, official statistics over time, or a peer-reviewed comparative study.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark not verifiable; 1 mark needs support [2] (b) 1 mark evidence; 1 mark why it is stronger [2]

items.stem: Assess the claim that statistics are always more reliable than personal testimony as evidence about the under-representation of women in parliaments.
items.answer: For: Large, representative samples can be generalised. Statistics can be checked and compared over time. Against: Statistics can be biased by sampling, question wording or presentation. Testimony shows experience and causes that numbers miss, e.g. eyewitnesses with ability to see. Judgement: Reliability depends on how the evidence was produced; the strongest case uses statistics and testimony that corroborate each other.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–5 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (6–8 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [8]

items.stem: What is meant by “turnout” in Global Perspectives?
options: The middle value when data are arranged in order, less affected by extreme values than the mean.
A statistical relationship between two variables, which does not prove causation.
The percentage of registered voters who cast a vote in an election.
A graph axis that does not start at zero, which can exaggerate differences.
items.answer: The percentage of registered voters who cast a vote in an election.
items.markingKey: Turnout: the percentage of registered voters who cast a vote in an election. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): A source with a vested interest is always wrong. Reason (R): Vested interest gives a reason to present information selectively. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: A false: such a source may still be accurate; it needs corroboration. R true. [1]

items.stem: Read this evidence about the spread of online disinformation during elections: “A campaign group in Mexico City predicts that, if nothing is done by 2050, this effect will become far more serious: “Trust in election results and in the media falls”.” Explain one strength and one weakness of this evidence.
items.answer: Prediction. Strength: it warns about possible future consequences. Weakness: it cannot be verified yet and comes from a campaign group with a purpose.
items.markingKey: 1 mark strength, 1 mark developed; 1 mark weakness, 1 mark developed [4]

items.stem: Donations (in thousands of dollars) received by 7 candidates in a local election in Kestria were: 29, 39, 9, 28, 480, 21, 18. What is the median donation?
items.answer: $28 thousand

items.stem: Election data for Dravonia: Year | 2010 | 2014 | 2018 | 2022. Overall turnout (%) | 70 | 64 | 61 | 55. Turnout aged 18–24 (%) | 39 | 34 | 29 | 33. The People’s Movement argues: “Young people are becoming more and more disengaged from politics, so voting must be made compulsory.” (a) Calculate the gap between overall and youth turnout in each year. (b) Calculate the change in youth turnout between 2010 and 2022 in percentage points. (c) Explain why the data alone cannot show that compulsory voting is the right response.
items.answer: (a) 2010: 31 points, 2014: 30 points, 2018: 32 points, 2022: 22 points. (b) 33 − 39 = -6 points. (c) The data describe turnout but not its causes or the effects of compulsory voting; evidence from countries that introduced it, and other options such as automatic registration, must be considered.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark method; 1 mark all correct [2] (b) 1 mark [1] (c) 1 mark data show what, not why; 1 mark need evidence about the policy; 1 mark alternative actions [3]
